stimuli: Startle tones; Exp I: 2-s vs 16-s intervals (n=72); Exp II: regular vs variable at 8-s mean (n=144)
endpoints: Startle amplitude; retest at 1 min and 24 h
result: 2-s spacing gave more decrement in training but 16-s spacing gave lower retest startle; regular timing gave more habituation than variable at matched mean
limitation: Artificial tones; startle reflex, not threat assessment

stimuli: Recorded distress squeal at 80 or 100 dB; Exp 1: 10 trials 3 min apart (n=8 per group); Exp 2: retention after 0, 1, or 7 days (n=120); Exp 3: daily trials (n=32)
controls: Synthetic mimic matched in burst timing
result: Natural squeal exceeded mimic at 100 but not 80 dB; all habituated rapidly; the 100-dB squeal recovered more after 1- and 7-day rests and habituated more slowly with 24-h spacing

stimuli: Natural distress squeal and mimic across contexts
result: Generalization of habituation across contexts depended on stimulus significance

stimuli: 2-min calls of 10 species (predators: barn, tawny, little owl, kestrel, fox), 60-70 dB, after 3 min of human voice; n=10 per group
controls: Human voice; non-predator calls (mallard, gull, oystercatcher, great tit, red deer)
endpoints: Cage-, self-, and call-oriented behavior; defense; food intake
result: Barn and tawny owl calls increased self-oriented, call-oriented, and defensive behavior; kestrel and gull calls also increased defense; tawny owl call reduced feeding by about half (t(18)=2.67)
limitation: Untreated DBA/2 mice showed no fear in a later study from the same group (per KindermannEtAl2009); gull effect attributed to attention

stimuli: Alarm calls (whistles, trills)
result: Heart-rate discrimination of alarm calls preceded behavioral discrimination

stimuli: Alarm calls varying in type, rate, and amplitude
result: Calls tracked risk rather than predator type; receivers used call rate as risk information
limitation: Observational and playback components; details nr

stimuli: Five calls about 3 min apart, each a repeated call of five chirps from a juvenile female, 84-91 dB; four of one exemplar, then a new exemplar from the same caller or a call from a different caller
result: Vigilance fell by the second call; a different caller restored it, a new exemplar from the same caller did not; neighbours' calls evoked longer vigilance than strangers' (trend, P=0.06)
limitation: About 14 receivers per series; juvenile females only

stimuli: Owl calls
result: Most species changed behavior; spiny mice responded less

stimuli: Conspecific and heterospecific alarm calls
result: Both species distinguished alarms from song and responded similarly to conspecific and heterospecific alarms

stimuli: Owl calls
endpoints: Freezing or flight; corticosterone or cortisol
result: Voles froze or fled and raised corticosterone; spiny mice raised cortisol without behavioral change

stimuli: Conspecific alarm calls
endpoints: Vigilance; run to cover; re-emergence latency; seed intake
result: Alarms increased vigilance, shortened the run to cover, delayed re-emergence, and reduced food intake

stimuli: Ten exemplars each of a reliable caller (paired with a stuffed badger except on playbacks 5 and 10) and an unreliable caller (no predator), 84-91 dB
result: Postural responses to the unreliable caller declined and differed from the reliable caller by playback 5 (P=.014) and 10 (P=.007); vigilance duration showed the same pattern only as a trend (P=.075)

stimuli: 17-20 kHz FM sweeps, 85 dB
controls: Home vs unfamiliar cage; prior shock
result: Cage familiarity and prior shock shifted responses between flight and freezing
limitation: Synthetic sweep, not a natural call

stimuli: Habituation-recovery alarm playback; juvenile vs adult-female callers; familiar vs unfamiliar callers
result: Habituation to one caller recovered with a new caller; juvenile calls more evocative; familiarity null (Z=-0.30, p=.767)

stimuli: Alarms from reliable vs unreliable callers; degraded (distant) vs intact calls; one vs two callers
result: Unreliable, distant-sounding, and two-caller playbacks were more evocative

stimuli: Chirps, whistles, chucks
result: Call types carried different information and altered vigilance differently

stimuli: 11-s alarm-call bouts originally elicited by humans, dogs, or coyotes; 45 dB at 50 m
controls: Rubber-toy sound matched in rhythm, frequency range, and amplitude
result: Playbacks reproduced the escape responses to the corresponding live predators: burrow diving (humans), running to burrow and standing at rim (coyotes), alert posture in place (dogs)
limitation: Hawk calls not played back; authors' referential interpretation

stimuli: Juvenile alarm calls with manipulated rate and bout length
result: Adults ignored rate and bout-length changes in juvenile calls

stimuli: Natural 22-kHz calls; 22-kHz sine tones; 22-kHz-range noise; other ultrasonic stimuli
endpoints: Defensive behavior; freezing; conditioning and extinction
result: No single stimulus altered defense in naive rats (n=9); pooled 22-kHz range increased freezing; learned 22-kHz fear unusually persistent

stimuli: 5-kHz, 20-ms, 85-dB pulses at 5 Hz (SD 140 ms) or 0.7 Hz (mean 1429 ms, SD 1368 ms)
result: Jittered timing prevented rapid amygdala habituation, increased c-Fos, and promoted avoidance
limitation: Artificial pulses; distribution shape not tested

stimuli: Natural 50-kHz calls; sine-wave approximations; 22-kHz calls
result: Natural and synthetic 50-kHz calls both induced approach, especially in adults

stimuli: 22-kHz calls; flat and FM 50-kHz calls
result: 50-kHz: approach and c-Fos in frontal cortex, accumbens, thalamus; 22-kHz: perirhinal cortex, amygdala, periaqueductal gray

stimuli: Tufted titmouse mobbing calls; hawk calls
result: Foraging changed more to titmouse mobbing calls than to hawk calls

stimuli: Repeated calls; primary vs later syllables
result: Primary syllables had especially strong alerting effects

stimuli: Alarm calls with added white-noise nonlinearities
result: Foraging fell more after calls with added nonlinearities
limitation: Abstract-level detail; repeated exposure not tested

species: Mouse (C57BL/6J), rat (Sprague-Dawley), pallid gerbil; all male
stimuli: 3-min calls of owls and raptors, 70-80 dB peak, 0.3-9 kHz; Exp 2-3: calls as conditioned stimuli with footshock (10 pairings or 1)
controls: Non-predator bird calls (chaffinch, blackbird, mallard, quail)
endpoints: Freezing; exploration; vigilant rearing; conditioned freezing
result: No unconditioned defense to predator calls in any species (power to detect 12% change in freezing); all calls conditionable after 10 pairings with no predator advantage; one-trial learning only for tawny owl, goshawk, and mallard
limitation: Mouse strain differs from HendrieNeill1991; conditioning tested in rats only

stimuli: 22-kHz calls from a fear-conditioned partner
controls: Naive receivers; auditory thalamus lesion or inactivation
result: Only experienced receivers froze; auditory thalamus required
limitation: Sender also showed other fear behaviors

stimuli: Trills (terrestrial predators) and whistles (aerial predators)
result: Trills raised cortisol; whistles were linked to slowed heart rate

stimuli: Conspecific and heterospecific alarm calls
result: Woodchucks increased vigilance to both, more to conspecific alarms

stimuli: Mother's vs other female's calls; colony vs non-colony callers
result: No differential response to mother's or colony members' calls

stimuli: 22-kHz and 50-kHz calls
result: No freezing; matched tones reproduced most firing differences between call types

stimuli: 22-kHz calls
result: Proposed that rats learn from their own 22-kHz calls (autoconditioning)

stimuli: Conspecific alarm; robin (sympatric), blackbird (allopatric, similar), honeyeater (allopatric, dissimilar) alarms
controls: Avian control sounds including robin song
result: Response varied with playback (chi2=19.68, p=.0014); robin and blackbird alarms like squirrel alarms; honeyeater less
limitation: Robin song not distinguished from alarms

stimuli: Natural 50-kHz and 22-kHz calls, ~69 dB, 15 s, 1-2 min intervals
result: 50-kHz calls increased approach and dopamine (n=12), both declining rapidly; 22-kHz and noise did not

stimuli: Predator calls during foraging
result: Increased vigilance, suppressed and delayed foraging; distance to refuge unchanged

stimuli: Sounds with context-specific meaning
result: Cortical activation depended on the learned meaning of sounds

experience: Footshock; laryngeal nerve transection vs sham
stimuli: 22-kHz playback in a novel context
result: Preventing self-vocalization did not reduce acquired call-evoked freezing

stimuli: Hawk call followed by bird chatter
result: Vigilance relaxed faster with bird chatter

stimuli: Chirps or whistles from unfamiliar callers; 49 syllables over 2 min; 80 dB at 1 m
result: Chirps reduced c-Fos in medial amygdala and superior colliculus; most regions unchanged

stimuli: Natural 22-kHz and 50-kHz calls
result: Natural calls usually produced larger effects, with similar directions; single housing enlarged several effects

stimuli: Pup-call temporal morphs (natural interval ~175 ms)
result: Experience broadened and shifted behavioral and cortical tuning

stimuli: Pup calls
result: Temporal association cortex contributes to auditory-driven maternal plasticity

stimuli: Crowned lapwing alarms; conspecific alarms
result: As vigilant to lapwing alarms as to conspecific alarms

stimuli: Calls of two owl species
result: Predator- and species-specific changes; moonlight and cover also mattered

stimuli: Self-administered playback of cagemate vs stranger 50-kHz calls
result: Preferred stranger calls; only stranger calls reduced cocaine intake; lesions abolished both

stimuli: 50-kHz calls
result: Approach habituated despite contingent social interaction

stimuli: White noise 70-96 dB (typically 90 dB, 6 s) predicted by a 5-s cue
endpoints: Accumbens core dopamine (voltammetry, n=21); avoidance; foraging; operant choice
result: Dopamine fell to noise and cue; did not scale with intensity (p=.88); unexpected noise slowed recovery
limitation: Freely moving; contrasts with FuruyamaEtAl2026 on intensity

stimuli: Partner vs stranger male calls, including calls directed at another female
result: Discriminated partner from stranger calls

stimuli: Noise bursts 45-105 dB, 10 s; ramped and damped noise
endpoints: Accumbens and tail-striatum dopamine (photometry); striatal neuron calcium; pupil; place avoidance at 85 dB
result: Accumbens dopamine fell more with louder noise (9 decrease-type mice); 6 others also showed an onset increase on the first burst; tail-striatum dopamine rose
